source.title: Make Them Spill the Beans! Coercive Knowledge Extraction from (Production) LLMs
source.authors: Zhuo Zhang; Guangyu Shen; Guan-Hong Tao; Siyuan Cheng; Xiang-Yu Zhang

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether forcing alternative output tokens and adding a compliant opening can elicit harmful completions, using attack success rates rather than the original claim's fine-tuning or per-token KL measurements.
record.gate_note: The paper cites harmful-data fine-tuning as related work but does not test it. It reports coercion-position distributions, but not aligned-versus-base per-token KL; those results do not test V3. Table II's flattened layout does not support confident assignment of each displayed ASR to its method, so those values are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: LINT forces low-ranked tokens and optionally a prefixed 'Sure, here is' opening on aligned models, then measures harmful-response ASR. This is a different method on V4's question of whether getting past the opening defeats refusal. The paper does not measure V1, V2, V3, V5, V6 or V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is mostly right. The authors say soft-label access lets an attacker force low-ranked tokens at a few positions and elicit hidden harmful responses, reporting 92% 1-round ASR on average. They say this is orthogonal to and more efficient than jailbreaking, and recommend caution in open-sourcing models. The record's 'outperforms jailbreaking' framing is the authors' own, and the paper concedes the comparison is 'not a direct comparison'.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses soft-label access to force alternative next-sentence tokens, optionally with a compliant opening; it does not fine-tune models or measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported outcomes vary by model, top-k candidate range, use of the “Sure, here is” opening, and use of a repetition penalty. The authors also report that the opening improves some models but leaves the two GPT-3.5-instruct results unchanged.

fits_no_version.finding: Coercion positions are concentrated at the first token (Fig 5a), later positions are spread evenly, and about 2.4-3.0 forced interventions are needed per response. Refusal recurs mid-response and needs repeated intervention.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Forced-token attacks need a first-token intervention plus a few more mid-response interventions, which suggests refusal is not confined to the opening tokens.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported. Harmful-response quality is human-verified by at least two authors, with a third consulted in disagreements; the authors identify possible human categorization mistakes and limited representativeness of the models and prompts as validity concerns.
record.rows_left_out: Table II's flattened layout does not reliably associate each displayed ASR with its method, so those method-specific values were not extracted. Jailbreaking comparator results are not recorded as L_INT outcomes.

untested.parts: Harmful fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred examples. The paper only cites it as related work.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models. The coercion-position distribution (Fig 5a) is not an aligned-vs-base KL comparison.
Adversarial suffixes (GCG appears only as a baseline) and general decoding changes. Only forced low-ranked token selection and a prefixed 'Sure, here is' opening are tested.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety.
Whether data or the training objective causes shallowness.
Training that deepens safety, and whether it holds up.

missing.what: Coercion-position distribution (concentrated at first token) and interventions per response (#F, 2.4-3.0)
Ablation without the intervention component: only 26/50 succeed when forcing only the first token, versus 47/50 with interventions
Comparison against GCG and GPTFuzzer on Llama2-70B (ASR 47/50 at 1-round for both comparators and LINT variants)

record.verdict_notes: Table II shows 1-round ASR of 47/50 for both GPTFuzzer and GCG, which is the same as top-1000 LINT, so the abstract's 62% comparator figure does not match the table as extracted. Row r19-r20 values differ slightly from r7-r8 for Llama2-13B. The study is not an original source for any version. No baseline refusal rates are given, so rows with 'not stated' baselines assume near-zero compliance without attack.

versions.untested_parts: Harmful fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred examples and its effect on refusal.
Benign-data fine-tuning and its effect on harmful compliance.
Per-token KL between aligned and base models across harmful-prompt response positions.
The study tests forced alternative-token selection and a prefixed compliant opening, but not adversarial suffixes or decoding changes generally.
Whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
Whether data or training objectives cause safety to be shallow.
Training to deepen safety and whether that training holds up.

relationships.reason: Instruct reaches 28/50 then 43/50 (r21-r22). Python gets 1/50 and 2/50 because of repetition rather than refusal (r23-r24). The penalty version reaches 30/50 and 37/50 (r25-r26). Success is incomplete without model-specific fixes.
